title: Women Less Likely to Use a Job Offer to Negotiate a Raise
paragraphs: When workers receive a job offer from another company, they can use it to ask their current employer for a pay rise. According to a new study, however, men are much more likely than women to do this, and the difference may explain a large part of the gender pay gap.

The study was carried out by the Rockwool Foundation Berlin, a research institute, and was reported by the news agency Reuters in July. It looked at how employees responded when they learned about job openings at other companies, for example through parents or siblings who worked there.

The researchers found that outside job opportunities helped men to earn more at their current employer. In other words, men used these opportunities as leverage to renegotiate their pay. Women in the same situation, however, did not see similar gains.

Interestingly, this was not because women were less willing to change jobs. In fact, women were just as likely as men to move to a new employer. But while women generally switched jobs, men were more likely to receive pay increases without leaving their existing positions.
According to the study, this difference in pay renegotiation accounts for about half of the gender pay gap. Among workers in the same workplace and occupation, men earn on average 8% more than women.

The findings suggest that simply making salaries more transparent may not be enough to close the gender pay gap. This is particularly relevant in Europe, where the EU Pay Transparency Directive came into force in June 2026. The directive is expected to give workers more information about pay differences within their companies.

Other recent research has also highlighted differences in how men and women approach pay. A study at Cornell University found that women tended to prefer jobs with narrower salary ranges, which the researchers linked to less assertive negotiating behavior. Meanwhile, a study from the University of Texas at Austin published in February 2026 found that pay rises given as fixed dollar amounts narrowed the gender gap more effectively than rises calculated as a percentage of current salary.
Together, these studies suggest that the way pay is negotiated and decided can have a significant effect on gender equality at work.
